graduation_requirements.raw_text:
In alignment with the State of Vermont's proficiency model, students will earn their diploma through completing courses, with
proficiencies embedded, at Springfield High School. By earning all required 27 credits, students will demonstrate proficiency in all
Springfield High School graduation standards (including both content standards and transferable skills). Please refer to the table below
for a specific breakdown of each content area.



 Graduation Requirements
 English - 4 credits

 Social Studies - 3 credits
 ● 1 course with proficiency tied to American history and government

 Math - 3 credits
 ● Algebra 1 required

 Science - 3 credits

 World Language - 1 credit

 Health - 1 credit

 Art - 1 credit

 PE - 1.5 credits

 Financial Literacy - 0.5 credits

 Electives - 9 credits

 Total: 27 credits

courses.description: In Cosmos “U,” students work with teachers across designated content areas, including English, Science, Social Studies, Math, Physical Education, and Art. This course is designed to offer a variety of flexible pathways to earn credit towards graduation or for enrichment purposes. The selection of particular content or transferable skills to be mastered will be decided collaboratively by the student, counselor, Flexible Pathways Coordinator, and teacher. As a central hub for flexible pathways, Cosmos “U” offers an adaptable environment tailored to each student's needs. Learning activities through Cosmos “U” provide a comprehensive range of options, which can include Dual Enrollment and Early College for higher education credit, independent passion projects and capstones, online learning through VTVLC and other approved programs, and hands-on internships or work-based learning experiences, alongside other Expanded Learning Opportunities tailored to student interest. Whether a student requires daily structure for credit recovery or a flexible schedule for advanced study, Cosmos "U" provides the resources and teacher oversight necessary for success.

courses.description: Students who enroll in Work-Based Learning (WBL) have the opportunity to take part in a job shadow(s) or internship(s) after spending time researching their career(s) of interest, writing a resume and cover letter, participating in mock interviews, and/or looking at the trends and outlooks in the job market. Through a combination of meetings with the WBL Coordinator, real-world application, and experiential learning, students will gain valuable insights into various industries, develop essential employability skills, and make informed decisions about their future careers.

This format is designed to enhance learning experiences beyond those available within the walls of SHS through the Vermont Virtual Learning Collaborative (VTVLC) or other approved online providers. courses.description: Through the State of Vermont Flexible Pathways Initiative, Springfield High School students are eligible to participate in Vermont's Early College Program during their senior year of high school. This allows students to complete their last year of high school (earning their diploma) while simultaneously completing their first year of college. Students may not enroll in any SHS classes as an early college student. However, they can still receive support (counseling, college advising, etc.) and may participate in SHS-based activities (sports, prom, senior trip, etc.). After early college acceptance, a student may request to complete early college work at SHS. With administration approval, these students must sign in and out at the office, work only in the library for half of the day, and arrange their own transportation. Funds are available to students accepted into full-time programs through participating colleges throughout the state and covers the cost of tuition for 12-15 college credits. courses.description: In this course students will learn to become competent and responsible drivers who are committed to improving driver performance throughout their lifetime. Topics will include alcohol and drug education, seat belt usage, zone control method of operation, risk management and other topics. All concepts and skills to be practiced in the car, will be first presented in the classroom. A partnership will be formed between the instructor, student, and parent/ guardian to help support driving skills. This course will build a foundation of driving skills that students can use throughout their lifetime of driving.
courses.credits_text: 0.5 elective credit upon completion of both classroom and in-vehicle requirements.
courses.prerequisites: Proof of an official driver permit (physical card present) is REQUIRED to be on file with the SHS registrar prior to August 15th for fall semester course enrollment and prior to January 5th for spring semester course enrollment. Temporary paper permits and/or email confirmations WILL NOT BE ACCEPTED. Students who do not produce an official permit (physical card) to the registrar on or before these dates will be unenrolled from the course in compliance with Vermont state regulations. Enrollment in Drivers Ed is based on Date of Birth and proof of a valid Vermont drivers permit. Due to high enrollment numbers and required driving hours, this course is limited to 30 students per semester.
courses.notes: Note: Daily participation and attendance are required.

courses.description: This course introduces students to high-school English through structured support in reading comprehension, vocabulary, writing conventions, and analytical thinking. Students read accessible versions of grade-level texts centered on the theme “Coming of Age” and build foundational skills in annotation, paragraph writing, and text-based discussion. Emphasis is on developing confidence and proficiency in reading and writing skills.
courses.prerequisites: Placement based on prior performance, assessments, and teacher recommendations

courses.description:
This course introduces students to high-school English through a series of thematic units that explore identity, growth, and the challenges of coming of age. Students read a blend of whole-class texts, short stories, poems, and paired nonfiction articles to deepen comprehension and build a foundation in literary analysis. Students will also practice developing claims, refining sentences, and improving writing through the full drafting and revision process. Daily independent reading is expected to strengthen fluency and stamina. This course prepares students for the demands of English 10, which will include the expectation of nightly homework completion. Throughout the course, students learn to:
• Annotate and analyze fiction and nonfiction texts
• Identify and trace central ideas across text sets
• Write narrative, analytical, and explanatory pieces
• Cite evidence effectively in their writing
• Participate in structured discussions and collaborative activities

This course challenges students with complex independent readings, literary criticism, and accelerated writing expectations. Students study the “Coming of Age” theme through high-complexity texts and produce analytical, argumentative, explanatory, narrative, and creative work. Students participate in advanced discussions and must submit required summer work before the first day of school. Independent reading and homework will also be a nightly expectation of students in this course.
courses.prerequisites: 8th Grade English teacher recommendation & completion of summer work

courses.description: This course continues foundational literacy development while exploring themes of tragedy, control, and catharsis. Students read accessible versions of anchor texts, develop structured analytical writing, and strengthen grammar, vocabulary, and reading comprehension. This course prepares students for English 11.
courses.prerequisites: Placement based on prior performance, assessments, and teacher recommendations
courses.notes: Duration: One Semester, meets daily

courses.description:
This course challenges students to examine how individuals respond to conflict, power, tragedy, and societal pressures. Through text sets that include drama, novels, informational texts, and primary-source documents, students explore themes of control, justice, rebellion, and moral choice. Students develop vocabulary, reading comprehension, and writing proficiency while engaging in inquiry-based projects. Independent reading and homework continue to be a core expectation.
Students build on English 9 skills by:
• Analyzing complex characters and themes across multiple genres
• Comparing perspectives across paired readings
• Writing clear, well-structured analytical, argumentative, and explanatory essays
• Incorporating research and nonfiction evidence into writing
• Delivering presentations and participating in Socratic-style discussions

This course extends the English 10 curriculum through more complex texts, advanced writing expectations, and AP-aligned reading lists. Students produce sophisticated analytical and argumentative writing, participate in sustained discussions, and will be asked to work and read independently at home. Summer work must be submitted by the first day of school for weighted honors credit.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Advanced English 9 or English 9 + teacher recommendation
courses.notes: Additional Requirement: Summer work

courses.description: This course supports students as they study American literature with scaffolding and accessible texts. Students analyze how culture, history, and identity shape the American story while strengthening vocabulary, reading comprehension, and structured writing. The course prepares students for English 12.
courses.prerequisites: Placement based on prior performance, assessments, and teacher recommendations

courses.description:
This course examines American literature and thought through units that connect historical eras with modern issues. Students read text sets that include novels, memoirs, speeches, poetry, short fiction, and paired nonfiction to explore themes such as freedom, identity, justice, and the American Dream. Students also build college- and career-ready writing skills by producing polished drafts and practicing revision routines. Independent reading and homework continues to be a core expectation.
Across the year, students will:
• Analyze how historical context shapes literature and cultural conversations
• Compare arguments and ideas across primary and secondary sources
• Write argumentative, analytical, and narrative essays with increasing sophistication
• Develop research questions and integrate credible sources
• Participate in discussions that challenge them to evaluate multiple viewpoints

This course mirrors a college-level literary analysis course. Students engage in close reading of complex texts, exploring structure, style, themes, figurative language, symbolism, and tone. Students write expository, analytical, and argumentative essays and prepare for the AP exam in May. Summer work is required for weighted credit. Independent reading and homework continue to be a core expectation.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Honors English 10 and summer work

courses.description: This course focuses on essential reading, writing, research, and communication skills. Students explore British and world literature using accessible texts and paired nonfiction. Writing instruction emphasizes paragraph structure, thesis development, practical/workplace writing, and evidence-based reasoning.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of English 11 and/or teacher recommendation

courses.description:
This course is a capstone course that brings together world literature, British literature, and contemporary global texts. Students explore broad themes such as power, morality, identity, cultural conflict, and the search for meaning through curated text sets, paired readings, and literary/nonfiction connections. This course emphasizes critical thinking, academic writing, global awareness, and preparation for college-level reading and communication. Independent reading and homework continue to be a core expectation.
Students will:
• Analyze how authors across time and cultures address universal human questions
• Compare multiple texts that express different perspectives on similar themes
• Write sustained analytical, argumentative, and explanatory essays
• Conduct guided and independent research
• Participate in structured debates, Socratic seminars, and presentations

This course emphasizes academic writing, research, information literacy, and revision. Students write college essays, literary analysis, reviews, and a research paper, while practicing the full writing process. This is the most advanced senior-year English option
courses.notes: Note: Potential college credit through Vermont State University

courses.description: This course provides students with a strong foundation in news writing, reporting, and media literacy. In this writing intensive course, students learn the fundamentals of journalistic style, including news values, interviewing strategies, source verification, Associated Press Style conventions, and the structure of hard news, features, sports, and opinion writing. Throughout the course, students practice reporting techniques, write publishable articles, analyze professional models, and participate in peer editing workshops. Students also learn the basics of layout, design, and newsroom ethics, as well as how to evaluate sources, avoid bias, and understand the role of journalism in a democratic society. Students who demonstrate strong writing, responsibility, and collaborative skills have the opportunity to earn a staff position the following year, where they will take on leadership and production roles within the Greenhorn student newspaper.
courses.notes: Section: English Electives (do not count toward the core English requirement)

courses.description:
Advanced Journalism functions as the newsroom and editorial staff of the Greenhorn, Springfield High School’s student newspaper. Students in this writing intensive course take on increasingly complex reporting, writing, editing, and production responsibilities, working under real deadlines to publish multiple issues throughout the year. Returning staff members may serve as section editors, senior reporters, or managing editors, guiding Intro Journalism students, coordinating story pitches, designing pages, and shaping editorial direction. This course is ideal for students interested in writing, media, communications, public relations, broadcasting, or any field requiring clear, persuasive communication.
Advanced Journalism students deepen their skills in:
• Investigative reporting and in-depth interviewing
• Multimedia storytelling
• Associated Press Style mastery
• Copyediting, fact-checking, and headline writing
• Layout and design using digital publishing tools
• Editorial leadership and newsroom management
• Ethical decision-making and responsible journalism

courses.description: In this course, students will develop their critical thinking abilities, argumentative skills, and listening skills. Students will also practice and improve their research skills, while learning to write and present speeches. Students will gain experience in both giving public presentations and learning from the presentations of others. By the end of the course students will be able to prepare for and participate effectively in a range of classroom conversations and debates. This course will prepare students for college and careers that demand the following: logical thinking, clear spoken expression, active listening skills, an ability to conduct research, and adaptation and collaboration working in teams. This course will provide a forum for students to practice and develop effective communication skills for the purpose of addressing diverse audiences with confidence and competence. Using a variety of instructional strategies students will learn to research, outline, and deliver speeches appropriate for the setting and population. Students will study speech fundamentals and delivery strategies and learn to adapt purpose and message based on audience analysis. Special attention will be given to critical listening skills and ethical considerations.
courses.notes: Section: English Electives (do not count toward the core English requirement)

courses.description: In this course, students will learn the principles and techniques of creative writing and actively participate in writing workshops. Students will read and discuss the styles and techniques of various writers and will begin to develop their own sense of style and voice in their own work. Students will have a choice of genre, theme, and topic to focus their study on. This course will focus on the creative writing process through the study of fiction and creative nonfiction. Students will analyze examples of varying genres and will have daily critical discussions. Writing workshops will deepen the students' understanding of the writing process, and will provide students with additional time to craft and share their work. Students are expected to participate in meaningful class discussions and formal/informal presentations. Students will write creative pieces daily, revise and edit consistently, and frequently read independently. Independent reading and homework are a core expectation.
courses.notes: Section: English Electives (do not count toward the core English requirement)

courses.description: Students will explore the dramatic arts through script analysis, performance, and production. They will bring the page to the stage by delving into acting, directing, technical theater, and playwriting. This course emphasizes creativity, collaboration, and confidence-building, culminating in a final production. This course is designed for motivated students who are eager to learn on-stage and backstage techniques and develop strong problem-solving skills. Throughout the year, students will learn to analyze, write, read, and produce plays while strengthening their public speaking, social, and collaborative abilities. Students will participate in a Fall production during the first semester and a One-Act performance during the second semester, performed for the school and community. Students taking the course in the second semester will focus more on playwriting and smaller productions. There is a required after-school/weekend commitment of 5–10 hours for dress rehearsals and performances. Additionally, students must attend live theatrical productions or watch films, culminating in play/film reviews.

courses.description: This ninth grade course is comprised of a comprehensive health curriculum, which covers concepts of wellness, assessing the various dimensions of wellness. Instructional units include: Goal Setting, Mental Health, Nutrition, Substance Abuse Prevention, Interpersonal Communication, Decision Making, and Fitness. Students will use critical thinking skills to discover ways for enhancing wellness, reducing risk of disease and promoting healthy behaviors for themselves and their families. Students will demonstrate their learning achievement through performance and/or cognitive assessments. Health Education prepares students to make healthy decisions and take healthy actions on matters concerning personal, family and community health. The goal is for students to become health literate and to use such information/skills in health-enhancing ways.

This course teaches students the skills necessary to weigh options, make responsible decisions and to develop behaviors that promote healthy and balanced lifestyles. Instructional units include: Healthy Human Sexuality, Analyzing Influences, Accessing Valid and Reliable Information/Products/Services, Sleep, Mindset, and Motivation. All students will learn the lifesaving techniques of Adult First Aid/CPR/AED through the American Red Cross (CPR certification is optional). By the end of the course students will be able to demonstrate the ability to practice health-enhancing behaviors that reduce risk and promote health. Students will demonstrate their learning achievement through performance and/or cognitive assessments.

In Honors Geometry, the concepts in this class will include: geometric vocabulary, angles, logic, geometric figures such as triangles, quadrilaterals, lines, etc., transformations, congruence and similarity, trigonometry, and circles. This class is designed to move at a faster pace in order to cover more content. This would be a great option for students who took Honors (previously Accelerated) Algebra I or are ready for more after Algebra I part 1 and 2. The curriculum is aligned with the expectations of the College Board AP Calculus course. This course contributes to academic distinction in STEM. AP Calculus AB is an introductory college-level calculus course. Students cultivate their understanding of differential and integral calculus through engaging with real-world problems represented graphically, numerically, analytically, and verbally and using definitions and theorems to build arguments and justify conclusions as they explore concepts like change, limits, and the analysis of functions. This course includes the following proficiencies: Calculus.

Students will interact more with The College Board AP Classroom website to facilitate this work and testing preparation. This course includes the following proficiencies: Calculus.

courses.description: In this course, students will learn basic chemistry and physics through inquiry. By the end of the course, students will have an understanding of the following physical science ideas: matter; force and motion; electricity and magnetism and energy. Students will learn Physical Science content as well as Science and Engineering practices.
courses.fulfills_text: This course is required for all first time 9th grade students.
courses.notes: This course is required for all first time 9th grade students.

courses.course_name: Honors Introduction to Chemistry and Physics (9th Grade)
courses.description: In this course, students will learn basic chemistry and physics through inquiry. Students will be challenged to achieve advanced levels of understanding that push beyond the standard Introduction to Chemistry and Physics expectations. By the end of the course, students will have an understanding of the following physical science ideas: matter; force and motion; electricity and magnetism and energy. Students will learn Physical Science content as well as Science and Engineering practices.

In this course, students will learn basic chemistry and physics through inquiry. By the end of the course, students will have an understanding of the following physical science ideas: matter; force and motion; electricity and magnetism and energy. Students will learn Physical Science content, as well as Science and Engineering practices.

Biology is the study of life. By the end of the course, students will have an understanding of the following ideas: structure and function; ecosystems, ecology, heredity, and biological evolution. Students will learn Life Science content, as well as Science and Engineering Practices.
courses.prerequisites: Grade of 1.5 or higher in Introduction to Chemistry & Physics 9 or Introduction to Physical Science
courses.notes: Note: Recommended for 10th grade

courses.description: In this course students will learn about the origin of the universe, the life cycles of stars, and about Earth’s history during the Precambrian Era. Students also learn about Earth systems and how energy is transferred through these systems. Students will learn Earth & Space Science as well as Science and Engineering Practices.
courses.prerequisites: Grade of 1.5 or higher in Introduction to Chemistry & Physics 9 or Introduction to Physical Science
courses.notes: Note: Recommended for 11th or 12th grade

courses.description: In forensics, students will discover how science plays a role in solving crimes. We will cover topics like collecting evidence, analyzing DNA, studying blood types, autopsies and dissection, and exploring past and current events. By the end of the course, you will be able to analyze and understand data from crime scenes, and you'll learn how to solve crimes using forensic science. We will use models, conduct experiments in the lab, and engage in discussions to apply science to real-life situations. This will help you sharpen your critical thinking skills and give you a glimpse into potential careers in forensic science. Students will learn Life Science and Physical Science content, as well as Science and Engineering Practices.
courses.prerequisites: Passing grade in Introduction to Chemistry & Physics 9 or Introduction to Physical Science
courses.notes: Note: Recommended for 10th-12th grade

courses.description: This general physics course introduces the student to basic kinematic physics. Topics include Newtonian mechanics, forces, circular, rotational and planetary motion. Students will learn Physical Science content, as well as Science and Engineering Practices.
courses.notes: Note: Recommended for 11th or 12th grade

courses.description: This course is an introduction to the concepts, principles and applications of chemistry. Topics of study will include: atomic structure, periodicity, structure of matter, thermochemistry, solutions, and equilibrium. Lab sessions will illustrate the principles of quantitative interpretation of data. Students will learn Physical Science content as well as Science and Engineering Practices.
courses.prerequisites: Passing grade in Introduction to Chemistry & Physics 9 or Introduction to Physical Science; Algebra II (can be taken concurrently)
courses.notes: Note: Recommended for 11th or 12th grade

courses.description: This course is a continuation of the introduction to the concepts, principles and applications of chemistry. Topics of study will include acids/bases, redox reactions, introduction to organic chemistry, and nuclear chemistry. Lab sessions will illustrate the principles of quantitative interpretation of data. Note that this course is reflected as Introductory Chemistry on the college transcript from Vermont State University. Students will learn Physical Science content, as well as Science and Engineering practices.

AP Biology is a year-long introductory college-level biology course. Students cultivate their understanding of biology through inquiry-based investigations as they explore the following topics: evolution, cellular processes, energy and communication, genetic information transfer, ecology, and interactions. Students will learn Life Science content, as well as Science and Engineering Practices.
courses.prerequisites: Grade of 3.0 or higher in Biology
courses.notes: Recommended: Chemistry I

courses.course_name: A Walk on the Wildside: Nature, Community, and Environmental Research
courses.description: In this class, we'll head outdoors to discover and study the local Vermont environment. We'll do research in the SHS Forest, look into how climate change affects Vermont communities, and explore the ideas of biomimicry--that is, engineering based on how living things are structured and what they do. Students will learn Earth & Space Science and Engineering content, as well as Science and Engineering Practices.
courses.prerequisites: Grade of 1.5 or higher in Introduction to Chemistry & Physics 9 or Introduction to Physical Science; the willingness to go outside for class in almost any weather.
courses.notes: Note: Recommended for 11th and 12th grade.

courses.description: In this course, students will explore cosmetics design through a hands-on DIY (do-it-yourself) approach. Using chemistry and the engineering design process, students will design and make cosmetics products such as soaps, lip products, scrubs, perfumes, and makeup. Students will learn Physical Science and Engineering content, as well as Science and Engineering practices.
courses.prerequisites: Passing grade in Introduction to Chemistry & Physics 9 or Introduction to Physical Science

courses.description: In this class, you'll get a taste of the world of engineering. We'll dive into designing and creating things like bridges, rockets and self-powered vehicles. You'll learn how to use engineering methods to make your creations even better. This course will teach you valuable problem-solving skills that will come in handy in future classes and real-life situations. Safety is a top priority, so you'll also be learning how to safely use different tools and materials. You will keep a detailed notebook to track all your engineering ideas and designs. Students will learn Physical Science and Engineering content, as well as Science and Engineering practices.
courses.prerequisites: Grade of 1.5 or higher in Introduction to Chemistry & Physics 9 or Introduction to Physical Science
courses.notes: Note: Recommended for 10th-12th grade; Students will be expected to use tools and materials safely and to keep a detailed Engineering Design notebook.

courses.description: This course offers a flexible, student-driven environment where students can learn science through non-traditional pathways. Specific scientific standards and proficiencies are mastered through a plan decided collaboratively by the student, counselor, Flexible Pathways Coordinator, and science teacher. This adaptable model supports a variety of goals, ranging from credit recovery for missed core requirements to enrichment opportunities such as independent passion projects, scientific research, capstones, or advanced studies in specialized fields that extend beyond the standard curriculum. Additionally, Cosmos “U” can provide targeted support for students engaged in career-based internships or online courses. Whether a student needs daily structure to catch up or a flexible schedule to dive deeper into a specific area of scientific inquiry, Cosmos "U" provides the teacher oversight and resources necessary to succeed.

This course focuses on developing the skills and tools necessary to be successful in future high school social studies courses. Students will explore topics in civics and current events to build stronger skills in research, critical reading, and writing.
courses.notes: Note: Required for Grade 9

courses.description: This course studies the recent past and what is happening now in order to begin to understand how the modern world works. Students will learn how to analyze what is going on socially and politically in today’s society.
courses.notes: Note: Required for Grade 9

courses.description: This course gives a more in-depth look at the topics covered in Modern Society. It studies the recent past and what is happening right now in order to begin to understand how the modern world works. Students will learn how to analyze what is going on socially and politically in today’s society.
courses.notes: Note: Required for Grade 9

courses.description: This Ancient World History course explores the foundation of human cultures through an in-depth study of major civilizations, including Mesopotamia, Ancient Egypt, Greece, Rome, China, and India. We will examine how geography, religion, social structures, economics, and cultural accomplishments shaped these societies and continue to influence the modern world. Each unit will incorporate comparisons to modern society, helping students draw connections between the past and present. By the end of the course, students will gain a deeper understanding of the lasting impact of ancient civilizations on contemporary life.
courses.notes: Note: Recommended for Grade 9

courses.description: This course looks at the history of the United States, starting with the end of the Civil War. Students will compare past events to what is going on in the world today. Students will conduct independent research, and write arguments about the past and the present.
courses.credits_text: 1.0 Social Studies (meets American history and government requirement)
courses.prerequisites: Modern Society, Introduction to Social Studies or Honors Modern Society
courses.notes: Note: Recommended for Grade 10 or 11

courses.description: Migration and immigration have been central in the making of American history and culture. It has changed the social, political, economic, racial, and cultural fabric of America and the world. In this course, students will look at the movement of people in the Americas and coming to the Americas from Columbus and the transatlantic slave trade to the many migrations since. Essential topics, readings, and multimedia provide historical context to current debates over immigration, migration, assimilation, integration, “legal” and “illegal” and citizenship. Students will research various historical push and pull factors in immigration and migration. Students will be able to analyze and articulate current events in immigration and connecting. Students will show their proficiency by being able to compare and contrast, and explain from several points of view, the history of immigration and what it means to be “American”. Students will be asked to connect community, personal, national, and international experiences.
courses.offering_note: Offered every other year (next offering is 2027/2028)
courses.notes: Note: Recommended for Grade 10 or above; Offered every other year (next offering is 2027/2028)

courses.description: In this course, ideas of Sociology and Psychology will be combined, where students will examine: ways that their brain works, ways that they interact with society, and ways that trauma impacts individuals. By the end of the course, students will be able to “ask good questions” about themselves and the world around them.
courses.notes: Note: Recommended for Grade 10 or above; There is a significant amount of reading, and the writing of a 5-page paper.

courses.description: Welcome to Modern History Through Film! This course examines American history from the 1940’s to the present through the lens of cinema. Film is not just entertainment—it is also a primary source that reflects the views, values, anxieties, and perspectives of the time in which it was made. Through analyzing films and film clips, we will develop critical thinking skills to understand how history shapes culture and how culture shapes our understanding of history.
courses.notes: Note: Recommended for Grades 11 and 12; There will be a significant amount of writing, reflection, discussion, and critique of ideas.

courses.description: In this course, students will examine the history, culture, environmental, social, religious, and contemporary aspects of East Asia focusing on Korea, Japan, and China. We will use literature, film, visual arts, and music as historical sources. Students will show proficiency by comparing and contrasting various eras and countries including our own, develop a research topic and questions based on their interests, and share their findings. By the end of the course, students will be able to critically discuss current international relations, human commonalities and differences, and their impact on the student’s own life.
courses.offering_note: Offered every other year (next offering is 2026-2027)
courses.notes: Note: Recommended for Grade 11 and 12; Offered every other year (next offering is 2026-2027)

courses.course_name: Save Your Money. Know Your Rights.
courses.description: Students will explore personal finance (budgeting etc.), basic economics, and how to participate in government - we will examine questions such as: Why do prices “keep going up?” Where is my money going? What does it mean to be a citizen? What are the responsibilities of a citizen to their government? What about a government’s responsibilities to its citizens? In this class, we explore these questions while asking students “what’s your plan after graduation?”
courses.fulfills_text: Recommended for Grade 11 and 12; This course meets the Financial Literacy requirement for the Class of 2027 and beyond
courses.notes: Note: Recommended for Grade 11 and 12; This course meets the Financial Literacy requirement for the Class of 2027 and beyond

Students are exposed to the psychological facts, principles, and phenomena associated with each of the major subfields within psychology. They also learn about the ethics and methods psychologists use in their science and practice. This course contributes to academic distinction in Wellness.
courses.credits_text: 1.0 credit (DE); 1.5 credits (AP, when taken with the lab)
courses.prerequisites: US History; teacher recommendation - attend required teacher meeting to be scheduled in late spring
courses.notes: Note: Recommended for Grade 12; Juniors pursuing early college or advanced learning may request enrollment, pending instructor; Catalog lists both a DE and an AP option

courses.description: This course offers a flexible, student-driven environment where students can learn Social Studies through non-traditional pathways. Specific humanities and social studies standards and proficiencies are mastered through a plan decided collaboratively by the student, counselor, Flexible Pathways Coordinator, and Social Studies teacher. This adaptable model supports a variety of goals, ranging from credit recovery for missed core requirements to enrichment opportunities such as independent passion projects, historical research, capstones, or advanced civic and global studies that extend beyond the standard curriculum. Additionally, Cosmos “U” can provide targeted support for students engaged in career-based internships or online courses. Whether a student needs daily structure to catch up or a flexible schedule to dive deeper into a specific area of historical or social inquiry, Cosmos "U" provides the teacher oversight and resources necessary to succeed.

This course builds on the skills and knowledge gained in middle school art. Students will learn how to use the creative process to create interesting and meaningful compositions. Students will create artworks in drawing, painting, and other media. This class has a strong emphasis on creative problem-solving and meaning making through visual arts. Proficiencies covered: create and respond.

In this course, students will gain the skills to draw realistically from observation as well as develop a personal style and voice in drawing media. Gesture drawing, contouring, perspective, and shading techniques will be explored through still life, portrait, and landscape drawing with a variety of drawing materials. Projects will be enriched with art history, presentation, and critique. Proficiencies covered: create, respond, and connect.

In this course, students will use several different painting techniques and mediums to create meaningful artworks. Acrylics, oils, and watercolors will all be explored to create works from observation, imagination, and photo references. Projects will be enriched with art history, presentation, and reflection. Proficiencies covered: create, respond, and connect.
courses.offering_note: Offered every other year (next offering is 2027-2028)
courses.notes: Note: Offered every other year (next offering is 2027-2028)

courses.description: In this course, students will use digital photography to create strong compositions with personal meaning. The course includes techniques for taking photos using digital SLR cameras and editing those photos using open-source software. When students leave this course, they will be able to take good, meaningful photos on any device. Proficiencies covered: create, respond, and connect.
courses.notes: Note: This course requires lots of work done outside of class!

courses.description: In this course, students will explore tools and programs for creating digital artworks. The course includes digital drawing, basic animation, digital photography and editing, and various types of digital design. The work for this course will primarily be done in ProCreate on iPads. Proficiencies covered: create, respond, and connect.

Advanced techniques in drawing and painting will be explored as will alternative media techniques. Students will examine their existing art portfolio and create new artworks in order to create a comprehensive portfolio for college applications. This course can be taken multiple times for credit. Proficiencies covered: create, respond, and connect.
courses.notes: Note: This course is designed for highly motivated visual arts students.

courses.description: This course explores ceramic hand-building and pottery wheel techniques. In this course students will create both functional and sculptural works. Due to the nature of the course being offered every-other year, if the course requests are greater than the number of seats available, priority will go to 11th and 12th graders. Proficiencies covered: create.
courses.offering_note: Offered every other year (next offering is in 2026-2027)
courses.notes: Note: Offered every other year (next offering is in 2026-2027)

courses.description: In this elective course, students will learn multiple ways of approaching drawing and composition. With a focus on drawing, students will use various sketching techniques and other methods for planning artworks. By the end of the course, students will work to improve their skills in drawing, composition, and creative problem-solving in visual art. Proficiencies covered: create.

This course offers a flexible, student-driven environment where students can learn Art through non-traditional pathways. Specific artistic standards and proficiencies are mastered through a plan decided collaboratively by the student, counselor, Flexible Pathways Coordinator, and Art teacher. This adaptable model supports a variety of goals, ranging from credit recovery for missed core requirements to enrichment opportunities such as independent passion projects, portfolio development, capstones, or advanced studio studies that extend beyond the standard curriculum. Additionally, Cosmos “U” can provide targeted support for students engaged in career-based internships or online courses. Whether a student needs daily structure to catch up or a flexible schedule to dive deeper into a specific medium or creative process, Cosmos "U" provides the teacher oversight and resources necessary to succeed.

This class is for students who are already playing a band instrument at Riverside Middle School and/or may have studied privately, new to the district, or if you're an upper classman who played at some point in your schooling. The class will help you refine your own personal skills, but will also combine those talents creating the new "Cosmos Band”. The class will cover musical fundamentals and explore many styles of music. These students will have performances throughout the school year
courses.prerequisites: Past experience playing a band instrument of at least one year.
courses.notes: Duration: Every other day for the year

courses.description: This class is for anyone who has the desire to sing in small groups and large group settings. Students will learn music and vocal fundamentals while combining their efforts to create a choir. Many styles of music will be explored, including musical theater. These students will have performances throughout the school year TBD.
courses.notes: Duration: Every other day for the year

courses.description: This class is for any student who wishes to test the waters in the world of music. They can explore the possibilities of starting an instrument with the potential of joining one of the performance groups in the future. Students will learn some of the basics of music structure and will be provided opportunities to try varied instruments and vocals to find out if they have the knack and desire to move forward in the music program.

This class is exactly like the title suggests. This is an opportunity to learn more about the history and styles of music in the world around us. You will study the evolution of music from Bach to Rock and how it relates to the evolution of societies around the world. We will study the big names and musical styles to create an informed consumer of the performing arts beyond High School.

An Introduction to Guitar class provides foundational skills for beginners, covering proper posture, tuning, basic chords, and essential strumming patterns for acoustic and electric instruments. Designed for beginner to novice, this course teaches students to read music, tablature, and chord diagrams to play simple songs, enhancing dexterity and confidence.

This course is an introduction to the Spanish language and culture. Students will start to develop the skills of listening, speaking, reading, and writing. Students will learn to understand and communicate in the language at a basic level with simple verbal and written responses. Foundational grammar, essential sentence structures, and everyday vocabulary will be taught in this course. Students will also be introduced to customs, traditions and everyday practices of the Spanish-speaking world. By the end of the course students will be able to engage in basic conversations about themselves. A combination of texts and supplementary materials is used.

Students will build upon the basic vocabulary and grammar mastered in Spanish I. Students will expand their listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills. In this course, the difficulty of grammar structures, writing tasks, and reading texts increases. Learning Spanish requires extensive exposure to the target language and getting used to communicating in that language. Students are encouraged to fully immerse themselves in the Spanish classroom. A combination of various texts and supplementary materials is used.

In Spanish III, students deepen their proficiency in listening, speaking, reading, and writing acquired in Spanish I and II. This course focuses on more advanced grammar, vocabulary, and sentence structures. Students will engage with authentic texts, explore diverse cultural themes from Spanish-speaking countries, and participate in conversations on a variety of topics. Emphasis is placed on developing fluency and confidence through consistent practice and interaction in Spanish. By the end of the course, students will be prepared to communicate effectively in various contexts and further their language studies. This course is dual enrollment through River Valley Community College.

In this course students will expand their language skills mastered in the previous years. More complex grammatical structures are introduced and vocabulary learned in previous years is expanded and recycled. Students are called upon to speak and write with more complexity and accuracy. During this course students make every attempt to communicate in Spanish with the teacher and peers. A combination of various texts and supplementary materials is used.

This course is designed for students who are interested in communicating in a world language at an advanced level. Students will acquire knowledge of thematic vocabulary and more complex grammatical structures. Students are asked to speak and write with more complexity and accuracy. This course will increase students’ ability to read and appreciate literary texts in Spanish. During this course students communicate in Spanish with the teacher and peers. At the completion of the course students are expected to be able to communicate with a native speaker about everyday topics.

In this course, students will work towards progress on their IEP Goals and Objectives. Both instruction and assessment will focus on developing the skills identified within student’s the IEP. Progress will be reported quarterly on the IEP. Instructional topics may include math, reading, writing, social emotional learning and executive function depending on the needs of the individual.
courses.prerequisites: Students MUST be on an IEP as this course is one method for receiving specialized instruction as outlined in the IEP.

courses.description: The Academic Resource Center, also known as ARC, is a classroom in which students in grades 9-12 receive additional resources and study strategies to further their academic potential and success. Weekly mini-lessons are provided to teach and provide practice in organization, study, and literacy strategies such as active reading, using graphic organizers as a pre-writing strategy, etc. The bulk of the time is given to students to work on their academic course work with assistance from the ARC teacher. The mission of ARC is to provide a space where all students feel safe to seek assistance on their learning journey in a welcoming and respectful classroom; it is a place where questions can be asked, concepts revisited and reviewed, and students’ work, with guidance, to reach their academic potential.
This course provides support and preparation for mainstream classes to students in which English is not the primary language spoken in their home.
courses.prerequisites: For students in which English is not the primary language spoken at home.

courses.description: In this course, students will be exposed to a variety of concepts to help them prepare for life after high school. Units may include topics in digital citizenship, media literacy, career exploration, executive functioning skill-building, and more. This course may include in-town field trips to the Department of Labor office and/or local industries.
courses.prerequisites: Aimed at 9th/10th grade students. Strongly recommended prior to completing a Work-Based Learning experience.

courses.description:
In this full-year course, students will learn and gain reading and writing skills in English in a manner designed to address their individual learning needs. This is a modified course that uses a variety of texts to address the PBGRs defined by Springfield High School. By the end of the course, students will develop their reading comprehension and writing skills (including but not limited to grammar, usage, and mechanics). Students will also complete a research project in which they will read for understanding, evaluate sources to determine their reliability, and develop writing pieces requiring them to synthesize information from different sources into a cohesive written report. Skills gained within this course will assist students after graduation in gaining meaningful employment or skills to continue on to post-secondary education. Reading, writing, language, and research proficiencies will be addressed in this course.
Part I will be offered to students in 9th and 10th grade and will focus on building formative and foundational skills. Part II will be offered to 11th and 12th graders and will focus on life skills, which will include, but not be limited to, resume building, reading for understanding, and formal writing.
courses.notes: Open to: All O.D.P. students and others as referred by SHS; Section: English

courses.description:
In this course, students develop foundational algebraic thinking and number sense needed for daily life and future employment. Instruction focuses on understanding numbers, operations, and patterns, with an emphasis on practical application rather than abstract theory. Students will:
• Strengthen basic math facts and operations
• Use calculators appropriately and efficiently
• Work with variables, simple expressions, and equations
• Explore ratios, proportions, and basic graphing
• Apply algebraic reasoning to real-life problem-solving scenarios Instruction is individualized and paced according to student need. Real-world examples and hands-on activities support comprehension and engagement.
courses.notes: Open to: All 9-10 ODP students and others as referred by SHS; Section: Mathematics Course Sequence

courses.description:
This course emphasizes spatial reasoning, measurement, and practical geometry skills used in everyday life and the workplace. Students learn to recognize and apply geometric concepts through hands-on and visual learning experiences. Students will:
• Identify and describe basic geometric shapes and figures
• Develop measurement skills including length, area, volume, and perimeter
• Understand time, scheduling, and elapsed time
• Apply geometry concepts to real-world tasks such as construction, layout, and design
• Use tools and technology, including calculators and measurement instruments Instruction is individualized, with a focus on functional applications that support independence and vocational readiness.
courses.notes: Open to: All 9-10 ODP students and others as referred by SHS; Section: Mathematics Course Sequence

courses.description:
This course builds students’ ability to collect, interpret, and use data to make informed decisions. Emphasis is placed on understanding information commonly encountered in the workplace and daily life. Students will:
• Collect, organize, and interpret data using charts and graphs
• Understand basic probability and risk
• Explore averages, trends, and comparisons
• Apply statistical thinking to real-world scenarios such as surveys, production data, and quality control
• Develop problem-solving and critical thinking skills Project-based learning is a core component of this course, allowing students to apply statistical concepts in meaningful, hands-on ways.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra Foundations or Geometry and Measurement
courses.notes: Open to: All 11-12th ODP students and others as referred by SHS; Section: Mathematics Course Sequence

courses.description:
This course focuses on practical financial skills necessary for independent living and employment. Students apply math skills through real-world financial decision-making and business-based projects. Students will:
• Develop budgeting, saving, and spending skills
• Understand banking, wages, taxes, and payroll concepts
• Explore personal finance topics such as credit, loans, and consumer responsibility
• Apply math skills through business simulations and projects
• Strengthen problem-solving, planning, and organizational skills Project-based learning is emphasized. Students may participate in small business projects (such as a bread, coffee, or popcorn business), allowing them to apply math, teamwork, and workplace skills in authentic settings.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra Foundations or Geometry and Measurement
courses.notes: Open to: All 11-12th ODP students and others as referred by SHS; Section: Mathematics Course Sequence

courses.description:
This course introduces students to basic life science concepts with a focus on health, human body systems, and everyday biological processes. Instruction emphasizes understanding how science connects to personal wellness, caregiving, and workplace expectations. Students will:
• Explore basic human body systems and personal health
• Understand nutrition, hygiene, and disease prevention
• Identify living vs. non-living things
• Learn about plants, animals, and ecosystems
• Develop observation and classification skills Hands-on activities, visual supports, and real-life examples are used to support comprehension and independence.
courses.notes: Open to: All 9-10th ODP students; Section: Science Course Sequence

courses.description:
This course focuses on foundational concepts of physical science that relate directly to everyday life and work environments. Emphasis is placed on safety, cause-and-effect relationships, and practical problem-solving. Students will:
• Identify properties of matter (solids, liquids, gases)
• Explore changes in matter and basic chemical reactions
• Understand forms of energy (heat, light, sound, electricity)
• Learn about forces, motion, and simple machines
• Apply science concepts to workplace and home safety Instruction includes hands-on experiments, demonstrations, and applied learning connected to real-world contexts.
courses.notes: Note: This and the previous foundational course will rotate years; Open to: All 9-10th ODP students; Section: Science Course Sequence

courses.description:
This course helps students understand the relationship between humans and the environment, emphasizing responsibility, conservation, and community awareness. Students explore how environmental decisions impact daily life and the workplace. Students will:
• Learn about natural resources and conservation
• Understand recycling, waste management, and sustainability
• Explore weather, climate, and natural hazards
• Examine human impact on ecosystems
• Apply environmental concepts to school, home, and community settings Project-based learning may include school or community sustainability projects, gardening, or environmental audits.
courses.prerequisites: Either Life Skills & Living Systems OR Matter, Energy & Safety (foundational courses)
courses.notes: Open to: All 11-12th ODP students; Section: Science Course Sequence

courses.description:
This course integrates science concepts with vocational skills and workplace applications. Students apply scientific reasoning to problem-solving, safety procedures, and technology use in employment-related settings. Students will:
• Apply scientific concepts to vocational tasks
• Understand workplace tools, machines, and basic technology
• Practice safety procedures and hazard awareness
• Explore cause-and-effect in real-world systems
• Develop inquiry and problem-solving skills Hands-on projects and simulations allow students to apply science knowledge in authentic vocational and life contexts.
courses.prerequisites: Either Life Skills & Living Systems OR Matter, Energy & Safety (foundational courses)
courses.notes: Note: This course will rotate years with the Environmental course; Open to: All 11-12th ODP students; Section: Science Course Sequence

courses.description: The first year course places an emphasis on transferable skills, how to be a good high school student, and how those same skills will help lead to success in the workplace. Students will examine their interests through a variety of activities and career interest inventories, and will start building goals for themselves as they start to think about life after high school. Sociology, Economics, and Inquiry proficiencies will be addressed in this course.
courses.notes: Open to: 1st year O.D.P. students

courses.description: During the second year of study, students will work on developing pre-employment skills such as understanding help-wanted ads, talking on the phone with an employer, completing different kinds of job applications, completing interest inventories, and building resumes. Students will also do some video job exploration, analyzing work expectations, available jobs they may not have considered, and educational requirements for a variety of rewarding careers. Sociology, Economics, and Inquiry proficiencies will be addressed in this course.
courses.notes: Open to: 2nd year O.D.P. students

courses.description: The final year of Pre-Voc is designed to prepare students for job placement and life after graduation. Areas of study will include: choosing an occupation, finding a job, keeping a job, and management of work and adult responsibilities, such as accepting constructive criticism and learning appropriate behaviors at the workplace. In addition, they will explore topics related to budgeting, basic credit/debit card skills, accessing community resources, and planning and preparing meals. By the end of the course, students will have an understanding of the components of an independent, adult life. Sociology, Economics, Inquiry, Number and Quantity, and Health proficiencies will be addressed in this course.
courses.notes: Open to: 3rd and 4th year O.D.P. students

courses.description: This is an orientation to shop safety regulations with units on measuring, using basic hand tools, and some power tools, and different building materials. Small projects will be the vehicle for learning individual and group skills. Students will learn about refinishing furniture and how they can flip furniture for personal use or for profit. Students will have a final project, which will require the use of a variety of tools and materials. Engineering, Modeling with Geometry, Create, Perform, Present proficiencies will be addressed in this course.
courses.notes: Open to: Grades 9-12 (preference to grade 9)

courses.description:
This course provides students with individualized, hands-on instruction in practical life skills needed for independent living and successful community participation. Students learn to plan, shop for, and prepare meals, maintain living spaces, manage personal hygiene and health, budget money, and organize recreation and leisure activities. Instruction emphasizes real-world application through classroom projects and community-based experiences such as visits to stores, laundromats, and other local resources, helping students build independence, problem-solving skills, and self-confidence.
ODP Life Management (Independent Living & Community Skills, Grades 9–12)
• Plan, shop for, and prepare meals independently
• Maintain personal living spaces and hygiene routines
• Budget and manage money for daily living needs
• Apply problem-solving and decision-making in community settings
• Organize and participate in recreation, leisure, and wellness activities
• Demonstrate independence, safety, and self-management in daily life
courses.notes: Open to: Grades 9-12

courses.description:
This is a two-part sequence in nutrition, food preparation, consumerism, and food presentation. Students are introduced to the concepts of safety and sanitation; food selection, care, storage, and proper usage; measurements, nutrition, baking basics, and simple food preparation. Health proficiencies are being addressed in this course.
Major Topics or Themes: (additional topics may be covered)
• Kitchen safety and sanitation
• Nutrition
• Reading recipes
• Using standard cooking measurements
• Baking
courses.notes: Open to: All O.D.P. students

courses.description:
On-the-Job Training (OJT) is a community-based learning experience designed to support high school students with disabilities as they develop the skills, confidence, and independence needed for successful employment. Through a combination of classroom instruction and supervised work placements, students gain real-world experience in job settings aligned with their interests, abilities, and long-term goals.
In this course, students learn essential workplace skills such as communication, problem-solving, teamwork, time management, and self-advocacy. Classroom instruction reinforces practical concepts including workplace expectations, safety procedures, professionalism, and career exploration. Instruction also includes foundational banking and financial skills connected to employment, such as understanding paychecks, using bank accounts, managing deposits and withdrawals, tracking earnings, and practicing responsible use of debit cards and other financial tools. Students apply both workplace and financial skills at their job sites with guidance from teachers, job coaches, and employer partners. The OJT program emphasizes individualized, strengths-based instruction with appropriate accommodations and gradual skill development. By the end of the course, students will have built a work portfolio, gained hands-on employment experience, and developed foundational work and money-management skills to support competitive employment or continued career training after high school.
courses.notes: Open to: 3rd-year O.D.P. students or 11th-grade status

courses.description:
This course focuses on understanding and managing emotions while building the interpersonal skills necessary for healthy relationships in all areas of life: with peers, family, teachers, supervisors, and community members. We will emphasize relationship skill building and maintaining by exploring concepts like empathy, perspective-taking, effective communication, and conflict resolution. The goal is for students to develop a strong sense of self, understand their social impact, and cultivate the skills to form and sustain meaningful, positive connections.
Key Skill Areas: Self-Awareness & Self-Management
• Identifying and labeling personal emotions and triggers.
• Developing appropriate coping and stress-reduction strategies.
• Understanding personal strengths and areas for growth. Social Awareness & Empathy
• Recognizing verbal and non-verbal social cues (tone of voice, body language).
• Taking another person's perspective in different scenarios.
• Showing respect and understanding for diverse backgrounds and viewpoints. Relationship Skills & Communication
• Initiating and maintaining positive conversations.
• Practicing active listening skills.
• Assertively communicating needs and boundaries.
• Offering and appropriately receiving constructive feedback. Responsible Decision-Making & Conflict Resolution
• Identifying problems in relationships and generating solutions.
• Using a step-by-step process to resolve disagreements respectfully.
• Understanding the importance of compromise and when to seek mediation.
courses.notes: Open to: 9-12

courses.description:
This course is designed to equip students with the "brain-based" skills needed to plan, organize, manage time, and successfully complete tasks in school, at home, and in future workplace settings. We will focus on developing the internal tools necessary for self-regulation and independent action. Students will learn practical strategies to improve working memory, task initiation, sustained attention, goal setting, and organizational habits. Mastery of these skills is crucial for transitioning from high school into adult life and employment.
Key Skill Areas: Organization & Planning
• Using planners/digital tools effectively.
• Breaking large tasks (projects, long-term assignments) into manageable steps.
• Organizing physical and digital materials (binder, drive). Time Management & Prioritization
• Estimating the time needed for tasks.
• Setting realistic deadlines and meeting them.
• Distinguishing between 'must do,' 'should do,' and 'can wait. Task Initiation & Sustained Attention
• Overcoming procrastination and starting tasks promptly.
• Minimizing distractions and maintaining focus.
• Developing self-monitoring strategies to check work. Cognitive Flexibility & Goal Setting
• Adjusting plans when faced with unexpected changes or setbacks.
• Using feedback constructively to improve performance.
• Setting and tracking simple, measurable short-term goals (e.g., SMART goals).
courses.notes: Open to: 9-12

courses.description: This is an introductory course that is designed to present students with an awareness of the process of film production by studying curriculum units focused on screenwriting, art direction, cinematography, visual effects, sound and music, and more. Students will view and analyze a variety of films, short subjects, animation, and documentaries. A final project in an area of film production chosen by the student is required.
courses.notes: Open to: Grades 9-12

courses.description: This course will be an in-depth overview of early American history through WWII. Units may include the European exploration (“discovery”) of America, the first European settlements of America, the triangle trade, the 13 original colonies, the American Revolution, the War of 1812. From there the Mexican-American , Civil, Spanish American Wars may be discussed ending with WWI and WWII. History and Civics proficiencies will be addressed in this course.
courses.notes: Open to: Grades 9-12

courses.description: A simple approach to understanding the world of visual arts. Students will be exposed to a broad range of imagery, media, artists, and periods of history. This course illustrates the meaning of art in social and cultural life throughout history. Students will learn about different media and styles. They will have the opportunity to experience hands-on learning by creating a variety of art projects. The goal is for students to become more confident in their visual literacy. Visual and Performing Arts, Respond, Connect Personal, Connect Cultural proficiencies will be addressed in this course.
courses.notes: Open to: Grades 9-12

courses.description:
This course provides explicit, individualized instruction in foundational literacy and communication skills necessary for academic learning, employment, and daily life. Instruction focuses on reading, writing, speaking, and listening through multi-sensory, structured, and functional approaches. Students will develop skills in:
• Letter–sound relationships and word recognition
• Reading comprehension using adapted and high-interest texts
• Functional writing for real-world purposes
• Oral communication and listening skills
• Vocabulary development and language usage Instruction is modified and paced according to individual student needs and aligns with Occupational Development Program goals and high school proficiency-based standards. Proficiencies Addressed
• Reading (Foundational and Comprehension)
• Writing
• Speaking and Listening
• Language This course may serve as an entry point into the ODP English Language Arts sequence and prepares students for continued study in ODP ELA courses.
courses.notes: Open to: Grades 9–12; Section: Basic Skills

courses.description:
This course provides students with explicit, individualized instruction in foundational and functional mathematics skills necessary for daily living and community participation. Instruction emphasizes number sense, problem-solving, and real-world application through multi-sensory and hands-on learning experiences. Students develop proficiency in:
• Addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division
• Money management and consumer math
• Time, calendar, and scheduling skills
• Using math to solve everyday problems in community settings Instruction is modified and paced according to individual student needs and aligns with Occupational Development Program goals and high school proficiency-based standards. Proficiencies Addressed
• Number and Quantity
• Algebra Foundations
• Geometry & Measurement This course may serve as a foundational entry point into the ODP mathematics sequence and prepares students for continued study in ODP Algebra, Geometry, Statistics, and Financial Literacy.
courses.notes: Open to: Grades 9–12; Section: Basic Skills

courses.description: During this intro students will explore several forms of multimedia with an emphasis on editing audio, video, and images. Students will explore software such as; Final Cut Pro, Avid Pro Tools, and Adobe Photoshop using tutorials designed to teach specific techniques related to Audio and Video Production.

Additionally, students will delve into the diverse range of rewarding career opportunities within the business field. The curriculum not only imparts essential business principles but also illustrates how these principles can positively impact both professional careers and personal lives.
courses.notes: Instructor: Ms. Cummings; Section: RVTC Foundation Courses (open to grades 9-12 for 2026-2027)

courses.description: Learn how to navigate today’s digital landscape! Get to know a computer and how it works and take it apart. Create websites as a portfolio of your explorations in the field of information technology. Design in Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator and take your file straight to production on the 3D printer. Make graphic designs with our laser cutter. Learn Python and programming languages. Make video games. Investigate cybersecurity and work with microcontrollers like Raspberry Pi and Microbits.
courses.notes: Instructor: Ms. Wilson; Section: RVTC Foundation Courses (open to grades 9-12 for 2026-2027)

Intro to Carpentry will give students the opportunity to explore the basics of the trade of carpentry through small building projects such as dog houses. You will learn to use power tools and the basics of how a structure goes together. Take the first step toward building your future!
courses.notes: Instructor: Mr. Chamberlain; Section: RVTC Foundation Courses (open to grades 9-12 for 2026-2027)

The primary focus is on practicing forensic science and analyzing physical evidence found at crime scenes. Students will be taught the basic processes and principles of scientific thinking so as to apply them to solving problems that are related not only to criminal investigation, but to all disciplines.
courses.notes: Instructor: Mr. Gould; Section: RVTC Foundation Courses (open to grades 9-12 for 2026-2027)

courses.description: Introduction to Culinary Arts gives students a sampling of many aspects of the food service industry. Students will be introduced to the various career opportunities as they learn basic cooking and baking skills while exploring one of the largest growing industries. Instruction involves lectures, demonstrations, skill development and practical application.
courses.notes: Instructor: TBA; Section: RVTC Foundation Courses (open to grades 9-12 for 2026-2027)

courses.course_name: Introduction to Advanced Manufacturing and Engineering
courses.description: Almost everything we touch, use and even eat on a daily basis is somehow connected to manufacturing. Manufacturing is the foundation for all other industries. Engineering is the application of scientific principles and practices to real world problems, to find solutions. Introduction to Advanced Manufacturing and Engineering provides tools and technologies to make these solutions a reality. You can’t have one without the other. This introductory course will allow students to explore the many types of engineering and manufacturing in a “hands-on” way. Students will design and build robots, program and fly drones, build single-cylinder motors and learn to use parametric modeling software and 3D printers. They will also learn how to use a variety of hand and machine tools to make products out of a variety of materials. This class is for anyone who has wondered how to take an idea from your head and make it a reality.
courses.notes: Instructor: Mr. Gray; Section: RVTC Foundation Courses (open to grades 9-12 for 2026-2027)

courses.description: This introductory course will provide a window into the world of healthcare. Participants will be able to experience the various aspects of the Health Sciences curriculum taught in Health Sciences Level 1 and Level 2 with interactive labs, hands-on exploration, and knowledge and skills. Students interested in pursuing a healthcare career will benefit from exploring this foundational program.
courses.notes: Instructor: Ms. Peck; Section: RVTC Foundation Courses (open to grades 9-12 for 2026-2027)

Introduction to Horticulture provides a strong foundation in essential topics such as photosynthesis, the water cycle, tree propagation, and the cultivation of flowers and vegetables. Students will explore wildlife and their habitats, develop bird-watching skills for data collection through Project Feederwatch, and gain introductory knowledge in wildlife identification, and habitat management. This course offers an engaging blend of science, nature, and practical application - perfect for students eager to learn by doing.
courses.notes: Instructor: Mr. Vicere; Section: RVTC Foundation Courses (open to grades 9-12 for 2026-2027)

courses.description: How do relationships affect the quality of life? You will use knowledge and skills in human development and family studies to enhance personal development, foster quality relationships and manage multiple adult roles. In small groups you will examine careers in the human services cluster including counseling and mental health, early childhood development, family and community, and personal care services. Learn about real-life topics such as relationships and communication, career choices, budgeting and personal finance, establishing a household, nutrition, drug and alcohol abuse and anything else you need to know – you just need to ask!!!
courses.notes: Instructor: Mrs. Lihatsh; Section: RVTC Foundation Courses (open to grades 9-12 for 2026-2027)

Students will then learn the safe and proper use of welding and fabrication equipment, residential wiring and plumbing. These proficiencies will be demonstrated by the completion of individual projects.

Once the classroom teacher feels you’re ready, you can be placed at a worksite related to your technical program. The work experience can be after school or during school as a substitute for part of your technical program. Work-based learning experiences may be paid or unpaid, depending on the placement. Students earn one additional elective credit for every 180 hours of time on the job (maximum of three credits per year). Students are required to document work hours; work hours may be transferable toward completion of Vermont Registered Apprenticeship Programs. Students must remain enrolled in an RVTC program and may not schedule other classes during RVTC program time to be in the Cooperative Education program.

courses.description:
In the Pre Tech program at RVTC, you get to tackle real-world problems and work with tools and materials hands-on. It’s all about building the skills you’ll need for your future career. In the first part of the school year, you’ll explore the different career clusters at RVTC and practice employable skills in each of those areas. The second half of the school year you will choose a career that inspires you and create your own project based on that career.
In Pre Tech, we team up with other RVTC programs to solve technical challenges. We also visit different local employers to help you discover some of the careers that suit you. From childcare to welding, computer disassembly to cooking, video shooting to designing and marketing products - we cover a lot! If you like mixing academic and hands-on learning, or are interested in technical education, or if you’re just trying to figure out your path in life, Pre Tech is the place to be!.
If you learn best by balancing academic and hands-on learning styles, or believe you have a future in technical education, or just want to figure out what to do with your life, then Pre Tech is the place for you!
